title: Units & Measurement Conventions in the Lab

references.label: General microbiology/quantitative methods references (ASM, FDA BAM, CLSI)

summary: The standard system of units (largely SI-derived) and conventions used to record volumes, masses, concentrations, and time in laboratory work, chosen for consistency and unambiguous communication between people and instruments.
explanation: Laboratory measurements rely on a small consistent set of base units — grams for mass, liters (and sub-units: milliliters, microliters) for volume, moles for amount of substance, and derived units like molarity (mol/L) for concentration — plus consistent prefixes (milli-, micro-, nano-) that scale by factors of 1000. Using consistent units and always writing the unit alongside a number prevents a huge and common source of laboratory error: a value with no unit, or the wrong unit, can turn a correct calculation into a badly wrong reagent concentration or dose.

comparison.example: g, mg, µg, ng — each 1000-fold smaller moving right
L, mL, µL, nL — each 1000-fold smaller moving right
M (mol/L), mM, µM; also %w/v, %v/v for simpler working solutions

commonMisconceptions: Assuming a value is 'obviously' in a certain unit because that's the unit usually used for that reagent — always confirm, since a decimal or unit-prefix slip (mg vs µg, mL vs µL) can be a 1000-fold error.
Treating %w/v and molarity as interchangeable without converting — they express concentration differently and are not numerically equal for the same solution.
